new_statements.rule_in_words: The opened part of the work (the full lexicon export) contains NO prose statement on stress; the front matter that would carry one is only in the PDF, which is could not be reached by automated download. What the export does give is an acute accent on the stressed syllable of almost every polysyllabic headword (1,204/1,220 two-syllable, 1,733/1,775 three-syllable, 710/746 four-syllable single-word headwords carry a mark), so stress placement can be read off the data. Tabulation over all 4,100 single-word headwords (script, counting each vowel letter or vowel sequence as one syllable, as Farr 1996 syllabifies): (a) all-light non-verb words: two-syllable words are marked initial 673 vs final 69; three-syllable words second 1,200 vs initial 92 vs final 1; four-syllable words second 286 vs initial 68 vs third 18; (b) in words containing a vowel sequence/long vowel (C)VV(V), the first such syllable carries the mark in 589/646 (91%), e.g. áafua, áanda, aráaregari, áubovana; (c) verb citation forms in -ari are marked on the suffix vowel -ári (afigári, angasaghári, misuregári: 3-syl second 280, 4-syl third 240, 5-syl fourth 100), i.e. suffix-anchored, not positional. Farr 1996's rule (initial in disyllables, second syllable in longer words, overridden by the first (C)VV(V) syllable; verbs stressed on the vowel-initial suffix) predicts the mark on 2,781/3,096 (89.8%) non-verb single-accent headwords; the ~10% residue is lexical, and the dictionary records minimal pairs distinguished only by stress (óka 'fish' / oká 'ridged gourd'; jóka 'mercy' / joká 'inside'; ófofo 'sweat' / ofófo 'cemetery'). So the placement the dictionary documents is: default initial in 2-syllable words and peninitial in longer words, a heavy (C)VV(V) syllable attracting stress, suffix stress in verbs, and a marked lexical residue. Reading given as weight-sensitive because the heavy-syllable override is the dominant non-default factor; this is an inference from the marks, not a quoted statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No statement available (front matter not opened). A small minority of long, mostly compound or verbal headwords carry two acutes (e.g. bandúvegári, gogóghombári, ámbokéna, gíferére; ~40 of 3,880 marked polysyllables), which may mark a second prominence, but the export gives no key.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically stressed residue of roughly 10% of non-verb headwords, including stress-only minimal pairs (óka/oká, jóka/joká, ófofo/ofófo, and béka 'mouth' vs biká 'sister-in-law' as in Farr 1996). Verbs: stress on the vowel-initial suffix (-ári) rather than by syllable count. The entry misuregári 'to mispronounce.. put stress in the wrong place in words' shows the compilers treat stress placement as contrastive/lexically fixed.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary covers Korafe-Yegha [kpr]; its lexicon and headword marks are for the Korafe variety (the export is titled 'Korafe' and gives Yegha only as a separate finder list 'Yegha - Korafe', alongside Ambe Dofo, Baruga, Hunjara, Kaina Ke, Karoto, Wedau, Motu and Tok Pisin finder lists). Farr 1996 likewise describes Korafe. Nothing opened describes Yegha stress separately.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress rules can be set up for most of the language. Verbs: initial syllable of the tense/aspect/ person of subject / mood suffix is stressed. Exceptions: Stress has a lexical function in today's past and some future indicative forms. [...] Other words: The first syllable is stressed in words with two syllables, and the second syllable is stressed in words with more than two syllables. Exception: Vowel sequences pull stress to them, so that it is usually the first syllable with a vowel sequence which is stressed.

tone_statements.quote: Phonemic stress with a low functional load has been reported to occur in at least Yekora, Baruga, and Korafe. [...] In the case of Proto Binandere, penultimate stress is assumed for two- and three-syllable words (at least in the case of non-verbs), based on the analyses of stress in the present-day languages; Suena, Zia, Binandere, Hunjara, Tafota Baruga, and Korafe all exhibit this pattern. [...] It is not clear whether tone was present in Proto Binandere. If it was, then it has apparently been retained in only two (though perhaps more) languages. readall_conflicts: The catalog's fixed: initial syllable record (the StressTyp2 entry for this language, 'In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the initial syllable', sourced to Farr & Farr 1974 and Gordon 2002) disagrees with every later Farr source: the 1996 ANU thesis p. 22 (held page scan, weight-sensitive tier file) states initial stress only for two-syllable words, second-syllable stress for longer words, both overridden by the first (C)VV(V) syllable, suffix-anchored stress in inflected verbs, and an acute-marked lexical residue (Farr's fn. 20 notes the 1974 paper had interpreted vowel length as word tone, i.e. the 1974 analysis is superseded). The 2008 dictionary's headword marks, read across all 6,949 entries, match the 1996 description (89.8% predicted; first VV syllable marked 91%; -ári verbs suffix-stressed; ~10% lexical residue with minimal pairs óka/oká, jóka/joká, ófofo/ofófo) and not the fixed: initial syllable record, except for disyllables where both agree. No source opened here states 'no stress' or tone; the dictionary's prose front matter remains unread (could not be reached by automated download PDF), so the dictionary's own wording of the rule is still unverified.
